# Chinese Steamed Buns


Chinese steamed buns, also known as mantous, are staples in the Chinese diet andfor good reason. They are fluffy, soft, and pair perfectly with whatever fillings and toppings your heart desires (or eaten plain! That's spectacular as well.) Made with only simple, affordable ingredients, mantous are uniquely simple because they don't need to be baked. No need to turn on the oven as they are steamed right on the stove in as big or small of a batch as you'd like. 

My goal was to finally nail down a mantou made with 100% whole wheat flour. When looking for recipes online, I found that most used all-purpose flour or only partially whole wheat flour. I also struggled with consistency - sometimes they would turn out fluffy and amazing. Other times, it came out gummy, wet, and felt like I had boiled the bread not steamed it. 

Therefore, I started playing around with different ratios that could produce a fluffy, whole wheat mantou consistently. I compared existing recipes online and used the general ratios as a starting point. Naturally, full credit to those recipe creators whose work I benefitted off from. Some of my favourite recipe sites include [What To Cook Today](https://whattocooktoday.com/soft-fluffy-chinese-whole-wheat-steamed-buns.html#recipe) and the [Hong Kong Cookery](https://www.thehongkongcookery.com/2018/05/chinese-steamed-buns-mantou.html).




# Recipe

This yields around 2-3 buns. Just scale the recipe as you'd like with the following ratios. 

- 100g whole wheat flour
- 65g water
- 1/2 tsp yeast
- 1 tsp sugar
- Pinch of salt

1. Combine all ingredients until well combined. The dough will be shaggy and rough
2. Knead the dough until smooth and gluten network is well developed. You will know it's ready when it can pass the windowpane test and the dough is able to stretch, instead of tearing. It normally takes me at least 15 minutes of kneading to achieve this.
3. Proof the dough until doubled in size. I like proofing it in the microwave with a cup of hot water or in a slightly warmed oven (the air fryer works great!). It should take around 60 minutes but it depends on the temperature - go by volume not time.
4. Deflate and shape dough into desired shape. If you would like a filling, add now
5. Proof again until puffy - also takes me around 30 minutes in a warm environment
6. Steam on high for around 8-10 minutes. Once done, turn off the heat and leave the buns to rest for at least 10 minutes. Do not lift the lid or else the shock of cold air rushing in will cause the buns to shrink
7. Enjoy! I personally love eating it with condensed milk, peanut butter, red bean paste, or some cheese.

# Graveyard

-------------------------

##### 75% Hydration 

- 100g whole wheat flour
- 75g water
- 1/2 tsp yeast
- 1 tsp sugar
- Pinch of salt

1. 30 min autolyse
2. Knead ~20 minutes with bit of flour to prevent sticking
3. 90 minute first rise
4. Punched down and shaed. 30 minutes proof
 
Came out dense and shiny instead of soft. Crumb felt gummy with high degree of elasticity and reminds me of an eraser. I think the hydration level is too high so it was difficult to develop the gluten. Potentially overproofed as well. Not much of a sweet flavor either.

  ##### 65% Hydration 

- 100g whole wheat flour
- 65g water
- 1/2 tsp yeast
- 1 tsp sugar
- Pinch of salt

1. Combine and knead until gluten well-developed
2. 1 hour rise in warm microwave
3. Punch down and shape. 30 min proof
4. Steam on high 8 minutes. 10 min rest afterwards

Result was much better. Bread felt much fluffier and didn't have that "damp" taste and feel to it. Still not very sleep but has a nice, slightly deeper flavour from the whole wheat flour. Not very sweet but was good if eaten with toppings.

###### Sourdough Discard 

- 100g starter discard
- 10g sugar (~1.5 tsp)
- 1/2tsp vital wheat gluten
- 10g water
- Pinch of salt

1. Combine and knead until gluten well-developed
2. 1 hour rise, 30 min proof
3. Steam on high ~10 minutes, rest for 20

Not the worst. If the goal is to use up sourdough discard in an edible manner, did great. It was passable as a bread but was on the denser side. Had a bit of that sourdough tang but nothing that peanut butter couldn't address. The vital wheat gluten made kneading very easy and gave it structure very quickly. Not sure it actually helped the end product however. 

-------------------------



##### 66% Whole Wheat

- 100g whole wheat flour
- 50g all purpose flour
- 10g wheat starch
- 100g milk
- 1/2 tsp vital wheat gluten
- 15g sugar
- Pinch of salt

Wanted to see how much better it'd be if I actually used some all-purpose flour. Didn't love this to be honest. The dough felt really dry, even though whole wheat flour should require more water? Maybe the all purpose flour absorbed the liquid much faster. It also tasted too milky to me? Maybe I'm just accustomed to the whole wheat flour taste.
